hints: Normal reaction on the $30^\circ$ inclined plane is $R = mg\cos 30^\circ$, so limiting friction is $F = \mu mg\cos 30^\circ$.
Set up equilibrium for the first case (10 N up the plane, slipping down $\implies$ friction acts up): $10 + F = mg\sin 30^\circ$.
Set up equilibrium for the second case (75 N up the plane, slipping up $\implies$ friction acts down): $75 - F = mg\sin 30^\circ$.
Add both equations to eliminate $F$ and solve for mass $m$, then subtract to find $F$ and determine $\mu$.
walkthrough:
Resolving perpendicular to the $30^\circ$ inclined plane, the normal reaction balances the perpendicular component of weight:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ$$
$$F = \mu R = \mu mg\cos 30^\circ$$

The component of weight acting down the line of greatest slope is:
$$W_\parallel = mg\sin 30^\circ$$

When the upward force is $10\text{ N}$, the particle is about to slip downwards, so maximum friction $F$ acts up the slope:
$$10 + F = mg\sin 30^\circ \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)}$$

When the upward force is $75\text{ N}$, the particle is about to slip upwards, so maximum friction $F$ acts down the slope:
$$75 - F = mg\sin 30^\circ \quad \text{--- (Equation 2)}$$

Add Equation 1 and Equation 2 to eliminate $F$:
$$(10 + F) + (75 - F) = mg\sin 30^\circ + mg\sin 30^\circ$$
$$85 = 2mg\sin 30^\circ$$

Substitute $m = 8.5\text{ kg}$ into Equation 1 to find $F$:
$$10 + F = 8.5 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 42.5$$
$$F = 42.5 - 10 = 32.5\text{ N}$$
